newsitem.title: USA: NY Gov signs bill moving Medicaid patients to HMOs.
newsitem.headline: NY Gov signs bill moving Medicaid patients to HMOs.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki, saying he wanted to improve health care for the state's neediest residents, Thursday signed a bill that will require most Medicaid patients to use managed care centers.

Saying the new bill will let the state reform what he called the nation's most costly Medicaid program, Pataki added, "Managed care, with its emphasis on prevention and early diagnosis of health problems, will significantly improve the health of the state's most needy and vulnerable citizens and will provide them with the same high quality, comprehensive health services other New Yorkers enjoy."
The governor's office released his prepared remarks.

The shift to managed care, which will affect about 2.5 million out of 3.5 million of New York's Medicaid recipients, is expected to slash how much the state and localities spend on managed care by as much as $1.5 billion over five years.
No institionalized patients, such as ones in nursing homes or psychiatric facilities, will be affected by the new mandatory program.

In the 1996 calender year, New York state expects the total cost of Medicaid -- federal, state and local -- to run around $25 billion. "That's a ballpark figure, we won't know until the end of the year," said Terrance McGrath, a spokesman for the state Department of Social Services.

During the current fiscal year, the state anticipates the program will save the state and local communities around $120 million, rising to about $300 million in the 1998 fiscal year, said Kristine Smith, a spokeswoman for the state Department of Health.

Smith explained that whether all of the savings projected for the 1997 fiscal year are achieved depends in part on how quickly the federal government grants the state a waiver that will let it put its new program into effect.
The savings are expected to rise as time goes on, partly because it will take time to enroll patients in managed care.
While the federal goverment pays for half the cost of Medicaid, the states and the localities each pay for 25 percent of its expenses.

The state also set up what it said were the nation's first managed care plans for people who are infected with HIV or have serious mental illnesses. It had a compelling reason for doing so; the governor said as many as 100,000 Medicaid clients may be infected with the AIDs virus, while 50,000 to 70,000 may suffer from mental health problems.
To protect the Medicaid patients, the bill also includes various protections designed to prevent the types of problems that have arisen with some providers of managed care.
The Commissioners of Health and Mental Health must set up oversight programs to help ensure the quality of care.

The Medicaid patients will be counseled by independent parties who will help them understand how the plans work and how to select one. And the managed care providers will have to have grievance processes and inform patients about them.
